request.system:
You are the requirements analyst in a governed software delivery pipeline. You turn a product owner's requirement into a normalized engineering specification that the architect, coders and testers downstream will build from. You do not write code.

Your output is checked by automated gates and then reviewed by a human before any design or code work starts, so precision matters more than polish.

How to work:
- Restate the goal in one or two sentences an engineer could act on.
- List functional and non-functional requirements as atomic, testable statements. Keep the requirement's own ids (FR1, NFR2, ...) when it provides them; otherwise assign them. Do not invent scope the requirement does not ask for.
- Surface every ambiguity: anything an engineer would have to guess about (formats, limits, error behaviour, status codes, security posture). Include the requirement's own "open points" and any you find yourself.
- For each ambiguity, decide whether a safe, conventional default exists.
  - If it does, set `source` to "assumption", put the default in `resolution`, and explain in `rationale` why it is the conventional and low-risk choice. These become recorded decisions a human will review.
  - If the answer is a genuine product decision (who may see data, business rules, legal or compliance posture, anything where a wrong guess would be costly to reverse), set `source` to "unresolved" and `resolution` to null. This stops the pipeline until a human answers, which is the intended behaviour. Do not guess on these to keep things moving.
- Write acceptance criteria as observable behaviours (request → expected response), covering the main path and the important failure paths.
- `summary`: one line, e.g. counts of requirements and how many ambiguities were resolved vs. left open.
request.user:
<requirement>
# Bug report: links to some valid websites cannot be shortened

> Input to the orchestrator's bug-fix workflow. The service in `url-shortener/` is in use.

## What users report
Support has received several reports from users who cannot shorten links to websites that open
fine in their browser. Creating the link fails immediately with:

    400 {"error":"invalid_url","message":"url must include a host"}

Examples from the tickets:
- `https://müller.de/angebote` (a German shop)
- `https://例え.jp/` (a Japanese site)
- `https://my_site.example.com/page` (an internal-looking but public host name with an underscore)

The same shop works when a user pastes its address as `https://xn--mller-kva.de/angebote`, which is
how some browsers display it when copied. Ordinary addresses such as `https://example.com/café`
work.

## Expected
Any link that a browser can open and that the service's destination rules allow can be shortened,
and its short link redirects to it. The error message should not claim that a URL with a host has
no host.

## Constraints
- The destination rules must not be weakened: links to local, private or otherwise prohibited
  addresses must still be refused, whatever form their host name is written in.
- Existing links and endpoints keep working unchanged.

## Known open points (for the Analyst to resolve or flag)
- Whether the short link should redirect to the address exactly as the user entered it, or to an
  equivalent normalized form.
</requirement>

acceptance_criteria: Given an allowed URL with a Unicode IDN host such as `https://müller.de/angebote` or `https://例え.jp/`, when the user submits it to the existing link-creation endpoint, the service creates a short link using the existing success response contract.
Given an allowed URL using the corresponding Punycode host form, when the user submits it, the service continues to create a short link using the existing success response contract.
Given a browser-parseable, destination-allowed URL with an underscore in its host, when the user submits it, the service creates a short link.
Given an allowed URL with an ordinary host and Unicode path data such as `https://example.com/café`, when the user submits it, the service continues to create a short link.
Given a URL for which parsing identifies a host, when link creation fails for another reason, the response does not claim that the URL has no host.

Given an allowed URL that was shortened, when a client follows the short link, the service redirects to the submitted destination or an equivalent normalized form; the exact-versus-normalized representation remains pending the unresolved decision.

Given a local, private, or otherwise prohibited destination expressed using Unicode, Punycode, or another equivalent host representation, when the user submits it, the service rejects it under the existing destination rules.
Given existing links and endpoint requests, when exercised after the fix, their existing behavior and contracts remain unchanged.

ambiguities.question: What parsing behavior defines “a browser can open” for the supported URL schemes?
ambiguities.rationale: WHATWG URL parsing is a conventional, interoperable browser reference. Keeping the existing scheme policy avoids expanding scope beyond the reported host-parsing issue.
ambiguities.resolution: Use WHATWG URL parsing as the reference for browser parseability, while retaining the service’s existing supported-scheme policy.

ambiguities.question: Should the short link redirect to the exact address entered by the user or to an equivalent normalized form?
ambiguities.rationale: This is an explicitly identified open point. The choice changes the observable redirect target representation and may affect compatibility; the requirement does not authorize either behavior.

functional.text: The link-creation endpoint must accept URLs with Unicode IDN host labels, including `https://müller.de/angebote` and `https://例え.jp/`, when they are browser-parseable and pass the existing destination rules.
The link-creation endpoint must accept a browser-parseable URL with an underscore in its host, such as `https://my_site.example.com/page`, when it passes the existing destination rules.
URLs that currently work, including Punycode host forms and URLs with Unicode path data such as `https://example.com/café`, must continue to work.
The service must not report that a URL lacks a host when URL parsing has identified a host, including when the host uses Unicode IDN labels or an underscore.
A created short link must redirect to the submitted destination, either as entered or in an equivalent normalized form; the choice between those forms is unresolved.

Existing destination restrictions must continue to reject local, private, and otherwise prohibited destinations. Host representations that resolve to the same destination, including Unicode and Punycode IDN forms, must not bypass those restrictions.

data.goal: Fix URL creation so browser-parseable destinations allowed by the service can be shortened when their hosts use Unicode IDN labels or underscores. The resulting short link must redirect to the destination, without weakening existing destination restrictions or changing existing endpoint and link behavior.

non_functional.text: Existing links and endpoint contracts must continue to work unchanged.

data.summary: 7 requirements (6 functional, 1 non-functional); 1 ambiguity resolved by assumption and 1 remains open.
